title: Dependency Injection Container Resolution Order
prompt: Simulate how a dependency injection container builds a service. Each registration is `{ token, deps, lifetime }` with lifetime `"singleton"` or `"transient"`; if a token is registered twice, the later registration wins. Resolve `root` depth-first: build each dependency in the listed order before the service itself, then record `"<token>#<n>"`, where `n` counts the instances built for that token (starting at 1). A singleton is built at most once and reused afterwards; a transient is built every time something needs it. Return `{ ok: true, created }` with the construction order. Stop at the first problem and return `{ ok: false, error }`: a missing registration is `"Missing registration: X (required by Y)"` (or `"Missing registration: X"` when the root itself is missing); a cycle is `"Circular dependency: A -> B -> A"`, listing the path from the first repeated token back to itself.

explanation.beginner: A container is a recursive function `build(token)`. Look the registration up (a Map from token to registration, filled in list order so a later one overwrites an earlier one). If it is a singleton that already exists, there is nothing to do. Otherwise first build every dependency, then 'construct' this service by adding `Token#n` to the created list, where n is how many of that token you have built so far. To notice a loop, keep a stack of the tokens you are currently in the middle of building: if you are asked to build a token that is already on the stack, you have gone in a circle, and the part of the stack from that token onwards (plus the token again) is the cycle to report. When anything goes wrong, throw a small error and catch it once at the top to return `{ ok: false, error }`.
explanation.junior: This is a post-order DFS with a 'currently visiting' stack, the same structure .NET's ServiceProvider and InversifyJS use. Check the singleton cache before the cycle check: a singleton that is already built cannot be part of a cycle in progress. Use the stack (an array) rather than only a Set because the error message needs the ordered path; `stack.indexOf(token)` gives where the loop starts, so `Root -> X -> Y -> X` is reported as `X -> Y -> X`. Transients make the output grow with the number of paths, not nodes: a transient shared by two consumers is built twice (the diamond test), which is exactly the behaviour that surprises people in production when a 'transient' holds an expensive connection. Throwing a private error subclass and catching only that keeps real bugs from being swallowed. Worst case is exponential in graph depth for transient-heavy diamonds; real containers cache compiled factories, but the construction order logic is identical.
